claim: Improvements in perception are frequently accompanied by decreases in correlated variability in sensory cortex.
source: Improvements in perception are frequently accompanied by decreases in correlated variability in sensory cortex.
evidence: This is a general statement about a relationship observed in the field, supported by multiple citations in the introduction.

claim: Overall changes in correlated variability should minimally affect optimal information coding.
source: This relationship is puzzling because overall changes in correlated variability should minimally affect optimal information coding.
evidence: This statement is supported by theoretical work cited in the manuscript.

claim: General decoders optimized for broad sets of visual stimuli better matched the animals' decoding strategy than specific decoders.
source: We found that general decoders optimized for broad rather than narrow sets of visual stimuli better matched the animals' decoding strategy, and that their performance was more related to the magnitude of correlated variability.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments and modeling.

claim: The performance of general decoders was more related to the magnitude of correlated variability than specific decoders.
source: We found that general decoders optimized for broad rather than narrow sets of visual stimuli better matched the animals' decoding strategy, and that their performance was more related to the magnitude of correlated variability.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments and modeling.

claim: The inverse relationship between perceptual performance and correlated variability can be explained by observers using a general decoding strategy.
source: In conclusion, the inverse relationship between perceptual performance and correlated variability can be explained by observers using a general decoding strategy, capable of decoding neuronal responses to the variety of stimuli encountered in natural vision.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Increases in perceptual performance correspond to decreases in mean correlation between responses of pairs of neurons to repeated presentations of the same stimulus.
source: Many studies have demonstrated that increases in perceptual performance correspond to decreases in a very simple measure of shared variability in a population of sensory neurons: the mean correlation between the responses of a pair of neurons to repeated presentations of the same stimulus (termed spike count or noise correlations, or rSC; Cohen and Kohn, 2011; Nirenberg and Latham, 2003; Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Cohen and Maunsell, 2011; Gregoriou et al., 2014; Gu et al., 2011; Herrero et al., 2013; Luo and Maunsell, 2015; Mayo and Maunsell, 2016; Mitchell et al., 2009; Nandy et al., 2017; Ni et al., 2018; Ruff and Cohen, 2014a; Ruff and Cohen, 2014b; Ruff and Cohen, 2016; Ruff and Cohen, 2019; Yan et al., 2014; Zénon and Krauzlis, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by numerous citations to previous studies.

claim: The axis in neuronal population space that explains the most mean correlated variability explains virtually all of the choice-predictive signals in visual area V4.
source: We recently found that the axis in neuronal population space that explains the most mean correlated variability explains virtually all of the choice-predictive signals in visual area V4 (Ni et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study by the authors.

claim: Neuronal population decoders that extract the maximum amount of sensory information for the specific task at hand can easily ignore mean correlated noise.
source: Recent theoretical work shows that neuronal population decoders that extract the maximum amount of sensory information for the specific task at hand can easily ignore mean correlated noise (Kafashan et al., 2021; Kanitscheider et al., 2015b; Moreno-Bote et al., 2014; Pitkow et al., 2015; Rumyantsev et al., 2020; for review, see Kohn et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple theoretical studies cited.

claim: Decoders for specific tasks can ignore mean correlated variability because it does not corrupt the dimensions of neuronal population space that are most informative about the stimulus.
source: Decoders for the specific task at hand can ignore mean correlated variability because it does not corrupt the dimensions of neuronal population space that are most informative about the stimulus (Moreno-Bote et al., 2014).
evidence: This explanation is supported by a citation to a theoretical study.

claim: The dimensions of the neural code that are optimal for general decoding of any stimuli might be very similar to the axes that account for mean correlated variability.
source: Our idea is that the dimensions of the neural code that are optimal for the general decoding of any stimuli might be very similar to the axes that account for the mean correlated variability, because mean correlated variability is well known to depend on all of the stimulus features for which the population of neurons is tuned (Cohen and Kohn, 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on known properties of correlated variability.

claim: Mean correlated variability is well known to depend on all of the stimulus features for which the population of neurons is tuned.
source: Our idea is that the dimensions of the neural code that are optimal for the general decoding of any stimuli might be very similar to the axes that account for the mean correlated variability, because mean correlated variability is well known to depend on all of the stimulus features for which the population of neurons is tuned (Cohen and Kohn, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: If observers used a general decoding strategy, their perceptual performance might be inextricably linked to mean correlated variability.
source: If observers used this kind of general decoding strategy, their perceptual performance might be inextricably linked to mean correlated variability (Ruff et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the general decoder hypothesis.

claim: Many studies that found performance increased when mean correlated variability decreased used a change detection task.
source: This test based on a single stimulus dimension is an important initial test of the general decoder hypothesis because many of the studies that found that performance increased when mean correlated variability decreased used a change detection task (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Cohen and Maunsell, 2011; Herrero et al., 2013; Luo and Maunsell, 2015; Mayo and Maunsell, 2016; Nandy et al., 2017; Ni et al., 2018; Ruff and Cohen, 2016; Ruff and Cohen, 2019; Yan et al., 2014; Zénon and Krauzlis, 2012).
evidence: This is a summary of previous studies supported by multiple citations.

claim: The effects of attention on the performance of the monkey's decoder did not match the effects of attention on the performance of the specific decoder.
source: Indeed, we found that the effects of attention on the performance of the monkey's decoder did not match the effects of attention on the performance of the specific decoder (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiological experiments, illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: The performance of the specific decoder was little affected by attention, while that of the monkey's decoder was strongly affected by attention.
source: Manipulating attention affected the performance of each decoder differently: the performance of the specific decoder was little affected by attention, while that of the monkey's decoder was strongly affected by attention.
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiological experiments.

claim: The large effects of attention on the physiological monkey's decoder were better matched by the similarly large effects of attention on the modeled general decoder than by the small effects of attention on the modeled specific decoder.
source: We found that the large effects of attention on the physiological monkey's decoder (Figure 3A) were better matched by the similarly large effects of attention on the modeled general decoder (Figure 3B) than by the small effects of attention on the modeled specific decoder (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing the electrophysiological data to the model results.

claim: The monkey's decoding strategy was most qualitatively matched to the modeled general decoder.
source: In other words, the monkey's decoding strategy was most qualitatively matched to the modeled general decoder.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of decoder performances.

claim: The performance of the physiological monkey's decoder was more strongly related to mean correlated variability than the performance of the physiological specific decoder.
source: Indeed, we found that just as the performance of the physiological monkey's decoder was more strongly related to mean correlated variability than the performance of the physiological specific docoder (Figure 3C; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for analyses per attention condition), the performance of the modeled general decoder was more strongly related to mean correlated variability than the performance of the modeled specific decoder (Figure 3D; see Figure 3—figure supplement 2 for trial-shuffled analyses).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the electrophysiological data analysis, shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The performance of the modeled general decoder was more strongly related to mean correlated variability than the performance of the modeled specific decoder.
source: Indeed, we found that just as the performance of the physiological monkey's decoder was more strongly related to mean correlated variability than the performance of the physiological specific docoder (Figure 3C; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for analyses per attention condition), the performance of the modeled general decoder was more strongly related to mean correlated variability than the performance of the modeled specific decoder (Figure 3D; see Figure 3—figure supplement 2 for trial-shuffled analyses).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the modeling analysis, shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The more general the decoder, the more its performance was correlated with that of the monkey's decoder.
source: We found that the more general the decoder, the more its performance was correlated with that of the monkey's decoder.
evidence: This is a finding from the physiological data analysis.

claim: The more general the decoder, the better it predicted the monkey's trial-by-trial choices on the median changed orientation trials.
source: Further, the more general the decoder, the better it predicted the monkey's trial-by-trial choices on the median changed orientation trials (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a finding from the physiological data analysis, shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The modeled general decoder better matched the attentional effects on the electrophysiological monkey's decoder than the specific decoder.
source: The modeled general decoder better matched the attentional effects on the electrophysiological monkey's decoder and, most importantly, was more strongly related to mean correlated variability than the specific decoder.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: The circuit model mimicked the correlated variability and effects of attention in the physiological data.
source: Our model mimicked the correlated variability and effects of attention in our physiological data.
evidence: This is a description of the model's capabilities.

claim: The circuit model produced neuronal tuning and covariance based on the constraints of an actual network capable of processing images as inputs.
source: Critically, our model produced neuronal tuning and covariance based on the constraints of an actual network capable of processing images as inputs.
evidence: This is a description of the model's design.

claim: Attention reshapes neuronal population activity to better align with a fixed readout mechanism rather than changing the neuronal weights of the observer's decoder.
source: A prior study from our lab found that attention, rather than changing the neuronal weights of the observer's decoder, reshaped neuronal population activity to better align with a fixed readout mechanism (Ruff and Cohen, 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study by the authors.

claim: Even with switched neuronal weights across attention conditions, the performance of the monkey's decoder was still higher in the attended condition.
source: They found that even with the switched weights, the performance of the monkey's decoder was still higher in the attended condition.
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study by Ruff and Cohen.

claim: Differences in the performance of the monkey's decoder across attention conditions may be due to differences in how well the neuronal activity aligns with a fixed decoder.
source: In other words, differences in the performance of the monkey's decoder across attention conditions may be due to differences in how well the neuronal activity aligns with a fixed decoder.
evidence: This is an interpretation of findings from a previous study.

claim: The findings support the hypothesis that observers use a general decoding strategy in the face of changing stimulus and task conditions.
source: Our findings support the hypothesis that observers use a general decoding strategy in the face of changing stimulus and task conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Studies using a variety of tasks have demonstrated a relationship between perceptual performance and mean correlated variability.
source: Studies using a variety of tasks have also demonstrated a relationship between perceptual performance and mean correlated variability.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple studies.

claim: Some studies of discrimination tasks suggest that the relationship between perceptual performance and mean correlated variability cannot be explained by a specific decoding strategy that maximizes the amount of sensory information extracted for the task.
source: Some studies of discrimination tasks suggest that the relationship between perceptual performance and mean correlated variability cannot be explained by a specific decoding strategy that maximizes the amount of sensory information extracted for the task (Clery et al., 2017; Gu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from previous studies.

claim: Other studies of perceptual performance have found that observers can achieve high levels of perceptual precision under certain circumstances.
source: On the other hand, other studies of perceptual performance have found that observers can achieve high levels of perceptual precision under certain circumstances (Burgess et al., 1981; Kersten, 1987).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from previous studies.

claim: As a decoder becomes more general to more stimulus features, its weights will have to depend on more and more tuning properties of the neuronal population.
source: As a decoder becomes more general to more stimulus features, its weights will have to depend on more and more tuning properties of the neuronal population.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the properties of general decoders.

claim: A fully general decoder of stimuli that vary along many feature dimensions would be one whose neuronal weights depend on the tuning properties of the neurons to all stimulus features to which they are selective.
source: A fully general decoder of stimuli that vary along many feature dimensions would be one whose neuronal weights depend on the tuning properties of the neurons to all stimulus features to which they are selective.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the properties of fully general decoders.

claim: The weights of a fully general decoder would depend on the tuning of all neurons to all of the stimulus features to which they are selective.
source: Therefore, the weights of a fully general decoder would depend on the tuning of all neurons to all of the stimulus features to which they are selective.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the properties of fully general decoders.

claim: A large number of studies have shown that mean correlated variability depends on tuning similarity for all stimulus features.
source: A large number of studies have shown that mean correlated variability depends on tuning similarity for all stimulus features (for review, see Cohen and Kohn, 2011; Ruff et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The decoding weights for a fully general decoder would depend on exactly the same properties as mean correlated variability.
source: The implication is that the decoding weights for a fully general decoder would depend on exactly the same properties as mean correlated variability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the properties of general decoders and correlated variability.

claim: The circuit model is the only model (to the authors' knowledge) that captures the effects of attention on correlated variability that have been frequently observed in electrophysiological data.
source: Further, this specific model is key to our study because it is the only model (to our knowledge) that captures the effects of attention on correlated variability that have been frequently observed in electrophysiological data (Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a claim about the uniqueness of the model used in the study.

claim: The effects of attention on many aspects of neuronal population activity have been well documented, including effects on neuronal firing rates and on both individual and shared trial-to-trial response variability.
source: The effects of attention on many aspects of neuronal population activity have been well documented, including effects on neuronal firing rates and on both individual and shared trial-to-trial response variability (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Cohen and Maunsell, 2011; Herrero et al., 2013; Luo and Maunsell, 2015; Mayo and Maunsell, 2016; Mitchell et al., 2009; Nandy et al., 2017; Ni et al., 2018; Ruff and Cohen, 2014a; Ruff and Cohen, 2014b; Ruff and Cohen, 2016; Ruff and Cohen, 2019; Zénon and Krauzlis, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The simulated neurons in the model captured many of the attention effects observed in electrophysiological data.
source: The simulated neurons in our model captured many of these attention effects (Figure 2D–F; Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a description of the model's capabilities, supported by reference to figures and a citation.

claim: In the presence of correlations between neuronal responses, specifically differential or information-limiting correlations, limits on decoding performance will be dominated by these correlations.
source: Much theoretical work has supported that in the presence of correlations between neuronal responses, specifically differential or information-limiting correlations, limits on decoding performance will be dominated by these correlations (Moreno-Bote et al., 2014; for review, see Kohn et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established theoretical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Removing correlations by shuffling trials results in linear growth in Fisher information with increasing numbers of neurons.
source: Removing these correlations by shuffling the trials results in many changes; in particular, our trial-shuffled data demonstrate the well-documented linear growth in Fisher information that is expected with increasing numbers of neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C; Averbeck et al., 2006; Kohn et al., 2016; Shadlen et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a finding from the trial-shuffled analysis, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The model reproduces the gain effects of attention on neuronal firing rates observed in electrophysiological data.
source: Our model reproduces the gain effects of attention on neuronal firing rates observed in electrophysiological data (Figure 2D) which, in the absence of correlations, increases the sensitivity of the population (Averbeck et al., 2006; Kohn et al., 2016; Shadlen et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a description of the model's capabilities, supported by reference to a figure and citations.

claim: General and specific decoder performances had indistinguishable relationships with the amount of correlated variability removed by trial shuffling.
source: In summary, general and specific decoder performances had indistinguishable relationships with the amount of correlated variability removed by the trial shuffling (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D, E), suggesting that decoder performance became dominated by attention-related firing rate gains intrinsic to our model.
evidence: This is a finding from the trial-shuffled analysis.

claim: Constraining analyses of neuronal data by behavior can provide important insights into the neurobiological mechanisms underlying perception and cognition.
source: These results demonstrate that constraining analyses of neuronal data by behavior can provide important insights into the neurobiological mechanisms underlying perception and cognition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's approach and findings.

claim: The subjects were two adult male rhesus monkeys weighing 8 and 10 kg.
source: The subjects were two adult male rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta, 8 and 10 kg).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: All animal procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees of the University of Pittsburgh and Carnegie Mellon University.
source: All animal procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees of the University of Pittsburgh and Carnegie Mellon University (Protocol #17071123).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for the study.

claim: Extracellular recordings were made from single units and sorted multiunit clusters in V4 of the left hemisphere using chronically implanted 96-channel microelectrode arrays.
source: We recorded extracellularly from single units and sorted multiunit clusters (the term 'unit' refers to either; see Ni et al., 2018) in V4 of the left hemisphere using chronically implanted 96-channel microelectrode arrays (Blackrock Microsystems) with 1 mm long electrodes.
evidence: This is a description of the recording methods.

claim: The population size of simultaneously recorded units was 8–45 units (mean 39) per day for Monkey 1 and 7–31 units (mean 19) per day for Monkey 2.
source: The population size of simultaneously recorded units was 8–45 units (mean 39) per day for Monkey 1 and 7–31 units (mean 19) per day for Monkey 2.
evidence: This is a description of the sample sizes in the electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Visual stimuli were presented on a CRT monitor calibrated to linearize intensity with 1024×768 pixels and 120 Hz refresh rate.
source: We presented visual stimuli on a CRT monitor (calibrated to linearize intensity; 1024×768 pixels; 120 Hz refresh rate) placed 52 cm from the monkey, using custom software written in MATLAB (Psychophysics Toolbox; Brainard, 1997; Pelli, 1997).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claim: The monkey's eye position was monitored using an infrared eye tracker.
source: We monitored each monkey's eye position using an infrared eye tracker (Eyelink 1000; SR Research) and recorded eye position, neuronal responses (30,000 samples/s), and the signal from a photodiode to align neuronal responses to stimulus presentation times (30,000 samples/s) using Ripple hardware.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The monkey received a liquid reward for making a saccade to the changed stimulus within 400 ms of its onset.
source: The monkey received a liquid reward for making a saccade to the changed stimulus within 400 ms of its onset.
evidence: This is a description of the behavioral task reward structure.

claim: Attention was cued in blocks of trials, with each block preceded by 10 instruction trials that cued one of the two stimulus locations.
source: Attention was cued in blocks of trials, with each block preceded by 10 instruction trials that cued one of the two stimulus locations by only presenting stimuli at that location.
evidence: This is a description of the attention manipulation in the behavioral task.

claim: In each block, the orientation change occurred at the cued location in 80% of the change trials and at the uncued location in 20% of the change trials.
source: In each block, the orientation change occurred at the cued location in 80% of the change trials and at the uncued location in 20% of the change trials.
evidence: This is a description of the attention manipulation in the behavioral task.

claim: The firing rate per stimulus presentation was based on the spike count response between 60 and 260 ms after stimulus onset to account for V4 latency.
source: The firing rate per stimulus presentation was based on the spike count response between 60 and 260 ms after stimulus onset to account for V4 latency.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

claim: Mean correlated variability of each pair of simultaneously recorded units was defined as the correlation between the firing rates of the two units in response to repeated presentations of the same stimulus.
source: We defined the mean correlated variability of each pair of simultaneously recorded units (quantified as the noise correlation or spike count correlation; Cohen and Kohn, 2011) as the correlation between the firing rates of the two units in response to repeated presentations of the same stimulus (the starting orientation).
evidence: This is a description of how mean correlated variability was calculated.

claim: For Monkey 1, two outlier points with mean correlated variability values greater than 0.35 were excluded from analysis based on the Tukey method.
source: For Monkey 1, two outlier points (uncued trials for each of 2 days) with mean correlated variability values greater than 0.35 were excluded from analysis based on the Tukey method (see Figure 3C for the range of included correlated variability values for Monkey 1).
evidence: This is a description of data exclusion criteria.

claim: The specific decoder was a linear classifier trained to best differentiate the V4 population responses to the median changed orientation from the V4 responses to the starting orientation presented immediately before it.
source: The specific decoder was a linear classifier trained to best differentiate the V4 population responses to the median changed orientation from the V4 responses to the starting orientation presented immediately before it (Figure 1D; first and second principal components shown for illustrative purposes only – analyses were based on neuronal population firing rates).
evidence: This is a description of the specific decoder analysis method.

claim: The monkey's decoder was a linear classifier trained to best differentiate the V4 population responses when the monkey made a saccade from the V4 responses when the monkey did not make a saccade.
source: The monkey's decoder was a linear classifier trained on the same set of V4 population responses as the specific decoder described above (the neuronal population firing rates in response to the median changed orientation and in response to the starting orientation presented immediately before it). However, unlike the specific decoder, the monkey's decoder was trained to best differentiate the V4 population responses when the monkey made a saccade indicating it detected the orientation change from the V4 responses when the monkey did not make a saccade (both correctly in response to the starting orientation and incorrectly when the monkey missed the changed orientation).
evidence: This is a description of the monkey's decoder analysis method.

claim: The network model is an extension of a previously published excitatory/inhibitory cortical network model of attention.
source: Our circuit model is an extension of our previously published excitatory/inhibitory cortical network model of attention (Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a description of the model used in the study.

claim: The network model consists of three modeled stages: layer 4 neurons of V1, L2/3 neurons of V1, and L2/3 neurons of V4.
source: Briefly, the network consists of three modeled stages: (1) layer (L) 4 neurons of V1, (2) L2/3 neurons of V1, and (3) L2/3 neurons of V4 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture.

claim: The L4 neurons of V1 were modeled as orientation selective filters with static nonlinearity and Poisson spike generation.
source: We modeled the V1 (L4) neurons as orientation selective filters with static nonlinearity and Poisson spike generation (Kanitscheider et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is a description of the model design.

claim: The model more than captured the electrophysiologically recorded attentional changes in V4 firing rates, mean correlated variability, and covariance eigenspectrum.
source: Finally, the model more than captured our electrophysiologically recorded attentional changes in V4 firing rates (Figure 2D), mean correlated variability (Figure 2E), and covariance eigenspectrum (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a description of the model's performance in matching experimental data.

claim: The model reproduces the relationship between noise and signal correlations observed in electrophysiological data.
source: Importantly, this model reproduces the correlation between noise and signal correlations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) observed in electrophysiological data (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Cohen and Kohn, 2011).
evidence: This is a description of the model's performance in matching experimental data.

claim: Attention weakened the relationship between noise and signal correlations in the model.
source: Using this model, we were able to measure the relationship between noise and signal correlations for varying strengths of attentional modulation. Consistent with the predictions of the general decoder hypothesis, attention weakened the relationship between noise and signal correlations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis.

claim: The difference in the attentional effects on the two modeled decoders decreased with larger population sizes.
source: But we also observed that the difference in the attentional effects on the two modeled decoders decreased with larger population sizes (right plot of Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis.

claim: The large attentional effects on the physiological monkey's decoders suggest that the monkeys were not working in the optimal regime near the saturation point.
source: What we do want to note, however, is that the large attentional effects on the physiological monkey's decoders suggest that the monkeys were not working in the optimal regime near the saturation point.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of decoder performances.

claim: The monkeys appear to have been working at an inner regime that allowed them to demonstrate large effects of attention on their performance.
source: Instead, the monkeys appear to have been working at an inner regime that allowed them to demonstrate large effects of attention on their performance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of decoder performances.

claim: The V4 neuronal population representations of the limited range of stimulus orientations tested in the behavioral task were reasonably approximated by a line.
source: For the physiological data, we again used linear decoders as illustrated in Figure 1D and E, as the V4 neuronal population representations of the limited range of stimulus orientations tested in our behavioral task (Figure 1B) were reasonably approximated by a line (Figure 3E; while a complex linear estimator was required for the modeled data based on the full range of orientations, linear methods were sufficient to capture decoder performance for the physiological dataset).
evidence: This is a justification for the use of linear decoders in the analysis.

claim: There was a significant correlation between decoder specificity level and the correlation with the performance of the monkey's decoder.
source: There was a significant correlation between decoder specificity level (x-axis) and the correlation with the performance of the monkey's decoder (y-axis; correlation coefficient: r=0.25, p=0.016).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis of decoder specificity.

claim: There was a significant correlation between decoder specificity level and performance predicting the monkey's choices.
source: There was a significant correlation between decoder specificity level (x-axis) and performance predicting the monkey's choices (y-axis; correlation coefficient: r=0.44, p=0.016).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis of decoder specificity.

claim: The correlation coefficients associated with the monkey's decoder and the specific decoder were significantly different from each other for Monkey 1.
source: For both monkeys, the correlation coefficients associated with the two decoders were significantly different from each other (Williams' procedure; Monkey 1: t=3.7, p=2.3 × 10–4; Monkey 2: t=3.2, p=1.4 × 10–3).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the comparison of decoders.

claim: The correlation coefficients associated with the monkey's decoder and the specific decoder were significantly different from each other for Monkey 2.
source: For both monkeys, the correlation coefficients associated with the two decoders were significantly different from each other (Williams' procedure; Monkey 1: t=3.7, p=2.3 × 10–4; Monkey 2: t=3.2, p=1.4 × 10–3).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the comparison of decoders.

claim: Within the cued attention condition, the performance of the monkey's decoder was more related to mean correlated variability than the performance of the specific decoder.
source: Within the cued attention condition, the performance of the monkey's decoder was more related to mean correlated variability (left plot; correlation coefficient: n=71 days, r=–0.23, p=0.058) than the performance of the specific decoder (right plot; correlation coefficient: r=0.038, p=0.75).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the cued attention condition.

claim: Within the uncued attention condition, the performance of the monkey's decoder was more related to mean correlated variability than the performance of the specific decoder.
source: The data within the uncued attention condition showed a similar pattern, with the performance of the monkey's decoder more related to mean correlated variability (n=69 days, r=–0.20, p=0.14) than the performance of the specific decoder (r=0.085, p=0.51; Williams' procedure: t=2.0, p=0.049).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the uncued attention condition.

claim: Randomly shuffling the trial order per neuron resulted in the Fisher information for the modeled general decoder increasing linearly with the log of the number of neurons in both the attended and unattended conditions.
source: Randomly shuffling the trial order per neuron resulted in the Fisher information for the modeled general decoder increasing linearly with the log of the number of neurons (dashed lines) in both the attended (yellow) and unattended (green) conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from the trial-shuffled analysis.

claim: Shuffling removes differential correlations, thus the Fisher information based on the trial-shuffled data does not saturate.
source: Shuffling removes differential correlations (Moreno-Bote et al., 2014); thus, the Fisher information based on the trial-shuffled data does not saturate.
evidence: This is an explanation of the trial-shuffled analysis results, supported by a citation.

claim: With shuffled data, the general decoder and the specific decoder behave very similarly.
source: The superposition of (A) and (B) illustrates that with shuffled data, the general decoder (large markers) and the specific decoder (small markers) behave very similarly.
evidence: This is a finding from the trial-shuffled analysis.

claim: A strong relationship between noise and signal correlations was observed in the recorded neurons.
source: We observed this strong relationship between noise and signal correlations in our recorded neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) as well as in our modeled data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiological data analysis.

claim: The data presented are from 46 days of recording for Monkey 1 and 28 days of recording for Monkey 2.
source: The data presented are from 46 days of recording for Monkey 1 and 28 days of recording for Monkey 2.
evidence: This is a description of the dataset size.

claim: Computer code for all simulations and analysis will be available at https://github.com/hcc11/GeneralDecoder.
source: Computer code for all simulations and analysis of the resulting data will be available at https://github.com/hcc11/GeneralDecoder; swh:1:rev:5056b409f2d943736b0478ff7ff38dd247b468b5, Ni et al., 2022.
evidence: This is a statement about code availability.
